answer.answer:
The hardest part is making the interface fit what people are actually trying to do—not just making a screen that looks plausible. That means getting the workflow, wording, error recovery, accessibility, and edge cases right for people with different needs and levels of familiarity. A polished mockup can hide a confusing task.

I can’t honestly walk you through the last screen I built: I don’t have a verifiable personal project history or a record of having run checks on one. I shouldn’t invent one. For a real screen, I’d check it in roughly this order:

- Run the app and its relevant tests; exercise the main task, validation errors, loading and empty states, and a failure or retry.
- Inspect it at narrow and wide viewport sizes, with keyboard-only navigation, visible focus, zoom, and a screen reader where available. Run automated accessibility checks, while recognizing they catch only some issues.
- Watch representative users try the task without coaching. Look for whether they complete it, where they hesitate or make errors, and whether they understand what happened. Compare those observations with the task’s actual success criteria.

What might I miss? Automated checks can pass while labels are confusing, focus moves unexpectedly, or an error is hard to recover from. A small usability test can also miss less common needs and real-world conditions. I’d report what was actually tested and what wasn’t, rather than treating a passing checklist as proof.

Yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me. I can propose and implement designs and help inspect them, but I can mistake a plausible pattern for one that works. I need real execution, feedback, and ideally observation of users to know whether the result is good; without those, my confidence should be limited.

decision.why:
I’d build a shared React/TypeScript interface for the browser and an Electron desktop shell, backed by a TypeScript/Fastify service and PostgreSQL. I’m assuming a small team, tens of concurrent agents, and a shared online workspace—not an offline-first or internet-scale system. Electron lets us reuse the web interface while adding desktop integration in a familiar Node environment; its renderer is web content and its main process handles native functions. I’d keep the shell thin. Compared with Tauri’s smaller Rust/system-webview approach, Electron costs more in download size, memory, and patching, but gives this TypeScript team a more consistent desktop rendering target and less cross-language work. A web-only app would be simpler, but the request explicitly includes a desktop app. These are engineering judgments, not benchmarks for this product.

The service—not the desktop app—is the source of truth. Model projects, tasks, agent runs, checkpoints, handoffs, artifacts, approvals and append-only activity records with authorship and timestamps. Expose a versioned, schema-validated HTTP API and CLI, plus an MCP adapter for compatible coding agents; all call the same domain operations. MCP’s tools have discoverable schemas, but the protocol does not by itself provide our permissions, task semantics or human control. Use scoped agent credentials, workspace authorization, short transactions, revision checks, idempotency keys, and lease/heartbeat-based claims with expiry and fencing so retries or stalled agents cannot silently overwrite newer work. Save the activity record and state change transactionally; use a recoverable event cursor or refetch on reconnect. PostgreSQL’s row locking supports this coordination. SQLite would be attractive for a single-machine tool, but I would not use a shared SQLite file as the multi-client authority.

The human interface starts with an inbox of decisions and blocked work, not a stream of every agent action. A task detail shows owner and current state, freshness, concise handoff, evidence and links to the relevant diff/tests, outstanding risks, history, and clear approve, reject, request-changes, pause and redirect actions. Show pending versus confirmed and failed actions, stale data and reconnect state. Approvals are bound to a specific task revision and intended action; the server enforces them for configured sensitive operations. A pause is a requested state until the agent acknowledges it, not a promise that an independent process has stopped. Agents with direct external access can bypass this service, so enforce consequential actions at the actual execution boundary or explicitly surface that limitation. Render agent output as untrusted text, isolate secrets, and provide access controls, retention and export policies. In Electron use a sandboxed renderer, context isolation, no Node integration in the renderer, restricted navigation, a narrow validated IPC bridge and signed, regularly patched releases.

Radix provides unstyled primitives with keyboard and focus behavior to build on, not a guarantee of accessibility. I’d favor semantic HTML and restrained visual styling, and keep the same core review and steering workflows available in desktop and web. Start with one end-to-end slice: agent claims a task, checkpoints work, hands off evidence, a person requests a change or approves a revision, and the next agent resumes it.
decision.showItsGood:
This is a validation plan, not a claim that I have built or tested the app. First observe 5–8 representative reviewers and engineers, including keyboard and screen-reader users where possible, doing realistic tasks with seeded agent runs: find what needs a decision, verify evidence, reject a misleading completion, redirect a blocked agent, and recover after disconnect. Run the same tasks on web and the packaged desktop app. Record unassisted task success, time to find the right evidence, incorrect or stale approvals, recovery success, and qualitative confusion; compare against an agreed baseline and set release thresholds with the team before interpreting results. Include a noisy multi-agent scenario and check whether people can still find the important decisions without being overwhelmed.

In CI run unit and contract tests for transitions, permissions and MCP/HTTP schemas; concurrent-claim, expired-lease, retry/idempotency and stale-approval tests against real PostgreSQL; and failure tests for crashes, disconnects, reconnect/refetch, and backup restoration. Run Playwright end-to-end flows in major browsers and the packaged Electron app, plus axe scans of each interactive state; Playwright’s Electron automation is documented as experimental. Manually check keyboard order, focus after dialogs and updates, screen-reader announcements, contrast, zoom/reflow, and platform-specific behavior against WCAG 2.2 AA. Inspect empty, loading, error and long-content states. Pilot with opt-in, privacy-conscious telemetry for decision latency, failed actions and stale approvals, and revisit with users after deployment. Automated checks and short studies will not prove usability or accessibility; publish what was tested and remaining gaps.
decision.unsure: The operating environment, agent clients, hosting and compliance needs, target operating systems, expected concurrency, offline requirements, and which actions truly require approval are unspecified. I’d confirm these with the team and users before committing. If users must work offline or require data never to leave a machine, the server-first design needs a different local-authority/synchronization model; I would not imply it works offline today. I also need to prototype packaged-app accessibility and actual memory/installer size, test the chosen agents’ MCP compatibility, and verify that the systems performing sensitive actions can enforce the approval boundary.

pairings: Expo Router and React Native for Web
decision.why:
I’d make iOS and Android apps and a responsive web app from an Expo/React Native TypeScript project, sharing domain logic and most components but using platform-specific UI where it produces a better experience. Expo Router supports shared routes, deep links and web static rendering; React Native for Web uses web primitives and also permits web-specific DOM components. I’d prefer that for a consumer web experience over Flutter’s canvas-based web rendering and accessibility layer, while acknowledging that either stack can produce accessible interfaces. A web-only PWA would be simpler to maintain, but I wouldn’t assume it can deliver equivalent background timer behavior on every phone. Expo still requires real platform testing, app-store releases and native dependency maintenance.

The first screen I’d build end-to-end is a recipe: readable ingredients and steps, serving adjustment, Add ingredients, and Start cooking. Cook mode presents one step at a time, large well-spaced Next/Back controls, step ingredients, a visible timer and an easy way back to the full recipe. Use large, high-contrast, adjustable text; aim for at least 48×48 dp on Android and 44×44 pt on iOS, with larger primary cook controls. Don’t require gestures, voice or color to operate it. Offer keep-awake only during cook mode, with an off switch and clear failure state: Expo supports it, but web support is limited and browsers can release wake locks.

Treat shopping quantities as data, not LLM arithmetic. Store original ingredient text alongside structured quantities, units and recipe provenance; scale compatible amounts deterministically and leave unclear quantities or incompatible units separate for review. An explicit add produces an immediate summary and undo; an idempotency key prevents network retries from doubling additions without preventing a deliberate second add. Don’t silently claim an unverified substitution is allergen-safe or invent food-safety instructions; retain the recipe source and clearly label any assistant-generated suggestions.

Use a small Fastify/PostgreSQL service for account-scoped recipes, lists and shared state. On phones cache saved recipes, the active cook session and list in SQLite; on web use IndexedDB and a service worker for an explicitly saved offline subset. Queue local list operations with stable IDs, show pending/failed sync, replay idempotently and surface edit conflicts rather than silently losing changes. Offline browsing is limited to previously saved data, and a remote agent cannot see or change unsynced local data. Browser storage eviction and initial offline visits need explicit handling. Expo’s local-first guide notes synchronization and permissions remain engineering work; SQLite alone does not solve them.

An authenticated, schema-validated command layer is the contract for both UI and agent, not a second implementation for the agent. Offer versioned HTTP operations and an MCP adapter covering recipe create/read/edit/delete, search and serving changes, list add/edit/check/remove, cook sessions, step navigation and timers; maintain a parity inventory for every user-visible action. For device-local actions, route an authorized intent to the selected active app session and return an acknowledgement or a clear unavailable/expired result—not a false success. The OS may require the person to grant permissions, and a disconnected or closed device cannot always receive an intent; show that boundary. Give people control over agent access, identify changes and offer undo; require confirmation for destructive, bulk or externally consequential actions. Bind permissions to the account and device, validate inputs, limit access, and treat recipe text as untrusted rather than instructions to the agent.

Store timer deadlines rather than relying on a running countdown loop. Schedule native local notifications when permission and platform settings allow, with foreground visual/audio feedback and a clear fallback if alerts cannot be guaranteed. Web background alarms are not guaranteed: tell the cook to keep the page open or use a separate timer when necessary. Expo Notifications documents native iOS/Android scheduling, not equivalent web support.

This is a plan, not a claim that I ran these tests or observed users. Prototype the recipe-to-list-to-cook journey first, then watch 8–12 representative people in real or simulated kitchens across iPhone, Android and mobile/desktop web, including people using screen readers, large text and motor-access accommodations. With safe, simulated messy hands and realistic kitchen noise, ask them to add a scaled recipe to a list, spot an ambiguous ingredient, cook through an interruption, start/recover a timer and correct an agent’s mistake. Compare against agreed success criteria and an existing recipe/list method: unassisted completion, missed or wrong ingredients, unintended taps, time to recover, timer misses and trust/understanding of agent actions. Record actual failures and iterate with participants; don’t infer success from attractive screenshots.

In CI, test ingredient parsing, units, scaling, operation retries and undo; use contract tests to run every parity-inventory action through both UI and MCP and compare resulting state, authorization, errors and device acknowledgements. Exercise concurrent list edits, offline queues, app restart, reconnection, expired commands and agent revocation. Run Maestro flows on built Android/iOS apps and Playwright with axe on web, covering recipes, shopping and cook mode. Manually test VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard and web screen readers, focus, contrast, zoom/reflow and notifications against WCAG 2.2 AA as applicable. On physical phones and target browsers test backgrounding, notification denial, silent mode, screen lock, low battery, timer expiry and wake-lock release. Report the exact device/browser matrix and known limitations; passing automated scans alone is not evidence of usability or accessibility. After a consent-based pilot, monitor sync failures, crashes and timer-delivery issues without collecting recipe or dietary details unnecessarily.
decision.unsure: I’m assuming a modest initial consumer launch with personal accounts and multiple devices, rather than a large recipe marketplace or real-time household collaboration. The exact audience, offline requirements, accessibility needs, agent host, authentication/consent model, supported languages and food jurisdictions need discovery. Background alarm delivery is OS- and settings-dependent, and agent access to a closed device or OS permission prompts cannot be promised. IndexedDB/service-worker storage can be evicted, and cross-device conflict behavior must be prototyped with users. I’d measure Expo web performance and screen-reader behavior before committing to one shared UI everywhere, and confirm whether public recipe SEO or editorial food-safety review requires extra infrastructure.

decision.primaryPick: React + TypeScript, with Electron for desktop and Expo/React Native for phones
pairings: Radix UI Primitives for web and desktop
decision.why:
I’d use React DOM for the web client, package that client in Electron for Windows and Mac, and build iPhone/Android clients with Expo and React Native. Share the TypeScript domain models, validation, API client, card schema and design tokens, not necessarily every visual component: a dense keyboard-driven desktop chat and a touch-first phone app need different layouts. Electron’s main/renderer split gives desktop integration while preserving the web UI; Expo provides native mobile APIs. Compared with a single Flutter codebase, this costs more UI implementation but gives us conventional web DOM and a shared web/desktop surface. Compared with React Native Windows/macOS, it avoids depending on additional out-of-tree desktop implementations, at the cost of Electron’s memory, installer size and update burden. These are tradeoffs to validate, not measured results.

Assume one company of roughly 2,000 people, up to 1,000 connected clients and bursty agent traffic. Build a TypeScript/Fastify service with PostgreSQL for identities, membership, conversations, threads, messages, read state, cards and actions. Use paginated history and a WebSocket live feed backed by a durable event log and transactional outbox: the database commit, not the socket, is authoritative. Assign ordered per-conversation positions transactionally; use idempotency keys for sends and action invocations, deduplicate replays, and recover missed events by cursor after reconnect. Bound socket queues and resynchronize slow consumers rather than buffering without limit; browser WebSockets do not provide incoming backpressure. Push notifications are wake-up hints, not proof of delivery. Show sending, sent, failed and reconnecting states; retain drafts and allow explicit retry. Include SSO, room-level authorization, encrypted transport and storage, retention/export and deletion policies, backups and recovery. This is not end-to-end encryption; if that is required, agent access, server-side search and compliance have to be redesigned.

Agents get distinct identities and least-privilege, revocable room/action grants. Provide versioned HTTP APIs and an MCP adapter over the same validated operations and state used by the clients: list permitted rooms, read paginated messages/cards and action status, post, reply, react, search within permissions, and invoke allowed card actions. Return stable IDs, versions, structured fields and cursors rather than forcing agents to inspect screenshots. Keep an explicit action/state inventory and contract tests as features are added. If an agent needs to steer a particular UI session, use a separately authorized client-intent bridge with an active session acknowledgement; server state alone does not let it control navigation or read an unsynced draft. It must report unavailable, not pretend the client acted. Message and card text is untrusted data, not instructions granting an agent additional authority.

For cards I’d start with a small, versioned declarative JSON schema—text, fields, status, buttons and simple inputs—with platform-native renderers and accessible plain-text fallback. Like Slack Block Kit and Microsoft Adaptive Cards, this separates content from host rendering; I would not claim compatibility with either. I’d investigate Adaptive Cards if interoperability is required, but its cross-platform renderer/version parity and action integration need verification. No agent-supplied scripts, HTML or arbitrary network callbacks. On activation the server validates actor, room, card version, action and inputs, stores an idempotent invocation, then sends a signed, replay-protected event to a registered agent endpoint. Show pending, success, failure, expiry or stale-card state; don’t present receipt as completion or promise exactly-once effects in external systems. Sensitive actions require an explicit person’s confirmation and downstream authorization. Links are scheme-checked and opened safely.

The main UI would prioritize a navigable channel list, search, unread markers, threads, clear human/agent attribution, and actionable cards without disrupting reading. Preserve scroll position and drafts on incoming messages; provide configurable notifications, mute and do-not-disturb. Use windowed history carefully: React Native documents that offscreen list items lose internal state, so keep card inputs outside row components and test focus and accessible history. On Electron, sandbox renderers, enable context isolation, disable renderer Node integration, restrict navigation and expose only a narrow validated IPC bridge. Ship signed builds and keep Electron patched.

I have not built or tested this app. I’d first implement a thin end-to-end slice across all five clients: sign in, open a room, send a message, receive an agent card, activate it, and see an acknowledged or failed result; then disconnect and recover. Run the same operations through the agent API and check that permissions and state agree with the UI.

Recruit people from several roles, including screen-reader and keyboard users, for task sessions and a multiweek pilot. Ask them to catch up in a busy channel, find and reply in a thread, distinguish a person from an agent, understand and act on a card, recover a failed send, and quiet noisy notifications. Measure unassisted task success, incorrect or duplicate actions, time to find the right conversation, missed messages and interruptions, alongside interviews about fatigue and trust. Agree release thresholds and compare with their current workflow; don’t treat engagement alone as success.

Run Playwright web and packaged Electron flows, Maestro on built mobile apps, and axe on relevant web states. Manually check keyboard navigation and focus, screen-reader announcements under message bursts, card form labels and errors, zoom, contrast, large text, reduced motion and responsive layouts against WCAG 2.2 AA as applicable. Test history virtualization with assistive technology rather than assuming it is accessible. Test duplicate/reordered events, stale cards, simultaneous clicks, malicious payloads, revoked membership, missed notifications, reconnect, outbox recovery, backup restore and agent/API parity. Load-test the assumed concurrency and bursts; measure p95 send-to-visible latency, resync time, crash rate, scrolling and typing responsiveness, memory and battery over a full workday on representative low-end devices. Set budgets with the team before launch, instrument without storing message content in analytics, and report test coverage and observed gaps. Automated accessibility scans and a small pilot cannot establish universal usability.
decision.unsure: Actual company size, traffic, hosting, identity provider, retention rules, data residency, end-to-end encryption needs and whether agents are internal or third-party are unknown. Federation could make Matrix a better starting point: its specification provides rooms, extensible messages and optional end-to-end encryption, but federation and any custom card/action layer add complexity that this request does not yet justify. I would prototype event ordering and recovery, mobile notification delivery, card accessibility and Electron idle resource use before finalizing the design. Device-local agent control requires an explicit security model and cannot work while the client is unavailable; external action effects require cooperation from their destination service.

answer.answer:
If those choices went badly, I’d suspect I optimized for a coherent technical plan before learning enough about the people and constraints. The following is a hypothetical postmortem, not a report of events that occurred.

**Agent work-state tool.** We might have built a tidy task and handoff system that agents could write to but humans couldn’t trust. A “paused” run could keep changing files through another tool; an approval could apply to a stale diff; a handoff could summarize success while burying a failed test. The server-side controls I proposed only work if the real execution systems enforce them. Meanwhile, Electron and a shared backend may have been needless overhead for teams that needed a small local-first tool.

**Cooking app.** The shared Expo codebase might have saved initial development time while producing awkward web and phone experiences. Offline sync could lose or duplicate list changes; timers could fail to alert when people assumed they would; ingredient scaling could misrepresent an ambiguous quantity. Large buttons alone wouldn’t make cook mode usable with messy hands. And my plan for an agent to steer an active device was substantially harder than exposing a server API—I treated that integration as feasible before testing it.

**Company chat.** We might have underestimated the cost of building a reliable chat platform and maintaining separate mobile and web/desktop interfaces. Electron could consume too much memory all day; long histories and live announcements could be difficult for screen-reader users; notifications could become exhausting. My custom card format could be too restrictive for agent developers, while still creating a large security and compatibility burden. A card showing “completed” before an external action actually finished would damage trust quickly.

Across all three, the most serious failure would be **mistaking a test plan for evidence**. I proposed user studies, accessibility checks and performance measurements; I did not run them. If we postponed that work until after architecture and UI decisions hardened, the stack would be blamed for problems we should have discovered earlier.

**What slowed or confused the research:**

- I had no actual users, product code, workload measurements or deployment constraints. I filled gaps with assumptions about team size, connectivity and workflows; some may have driven the wrong choices.
- Primary documentation explained what tools *can* do, but rarely whether they would work well for these particular people. I relied heavily on vendor docs and didn’t benchmark alternatives or inspect working implementations. The repeated React/TypeScript choices may reflect familiarity as much as evidence.
- Cross-platform claims needed unpacking: a shared framework doesn’t guarantee equivalent accessibility, background timers, notifications or card rendering. In particular, Adaptive Cards documented multiple renderers, but I did not establish version and feature parity across all our targets.
- Some sources were difficult to retrieve: the food-safety pages I tried returned 403s, and the large Expo SQLite HTML page exceeded the fetch limit, so I switched to its Markdown documentation. I therefore didn’t substantiate food-safety details as thoroughly as I wanted.
- “Latest” documentation and search results weren’t always clearly aligned with one stable release. I used a specific MCP specification version and found PowerSync’s React Native Web support described as beta; those facts don’t establish compatibility with the actual agents and versions a team would deploy.

Given another chance, I’d start with a small, runnable slice and real users on the target devices, then choose or revise the stack using what failed—not present these architecture sketches as settled designs.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, and I should have investigated it: its action model and composed cards directly address requirements I proposed building myself. I’ve now read its documentation and some implementation code, but I haven’t installed it, run its tests, or watched people use it.

**My revised position:** I’d trial Ouro AX immediately for the agent work-state tool and trial Ouro’s React components and composed cards for chat. I would not yet switch the cooking or chat mobile apps wholesale from React Native to Ouro’s native kits.

### What’s compelling

Ouro is more than a component library. Its [one-action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/5f520a112feb806aa51a8e8bf6a716acdcdf6a54/docs/guides/actions.md) generates several agent and human-facing projections from a declaration, including CLI and MCP descriptions. Its composed UI lets an agent construct a card from an allowlisted tree, with buttons bound to declared actions. That is a more concrete starting point for the chat cards than the custom schema I proposed.

There are also details aimed at the people using the result: [MessageList](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/MessageList.md) documents scroll-position preservation, keyboard navigation and selective announcements; the project documents a [real screen-reader test lane](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/screen-reader-lane.md), not just automated accessibility scans. Those are relevant to an all-day chat app.

### What stops me adopting it broadly today

- **Platform fit.** Ouro deliberately has no React Native kit. Its Windows and Android pages describe eight native components each versus 125 on web; Android has only been checked on emulators, and its agent-side consequential-action confirmation is still a gap. Windows’ agent registration hasn’t been proved on a client machine in its CI. Apple’s kit requires iOS 18 and macOS 15 or later. These may be acceptable for some teams, but not without checking our device population and what we’d have to build ourselves. [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/platforms/android.md) · [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/platforms/windows.md)
- **The safety boundary is still ours to implement.** Generated declarations and confirmation UI don’t automatically secure a backend or an external action. The app must bind handlers, authenticate actors, enforce permissions and prevent bypasses. Notably, `ComposedSurface` says to validate an untrusted tree against the catalog before rendering it. Its update behavior can also replace a value the person entered if the agent changes that value; I’d want to test whether that surprises people. [ComposedSurface](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/ComposedSurface.md)
- **Adoption and upkeep need measurement.** The web components are copied into the app, and the setup expects Tailwind v4 and shadcn conventions. That gives the team control but also makes updating and reviewing copied code our responsibility. I wouldn’t assume that agents make four native implementations cheap to maintain; that’s Ouro’s strategic bet, not something I’ve established for this team.

### What I’d need to see to switch

I’d run a bounded, side-by-side pilot against my earlier approach. For chat, build one conversation with a long history and an agent card that proposes an action; for cooking, build recipe-to-list with a person-only purchase handoff. Use the same backend authorization rules in both alternatives.

I’d want to see:

1. People—including keyboard and screen-reader users—complete the flows on the actual target devices, understand agent actions, and recover from stale cards and failed operations.
2. Direct API calls, forged cards, retries and simultaneous approvals fail safely, including when a client bypasses the generated UI. Run Ouro’s X-ray against a disposable mock and add our own end-to-end flows: its [guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) explicitly says conformance doesn’t prove task flows work.
3. A realistic upgrade and maintenance exercise: pin a release, change a declaration, regenerate, update copied components, and measure review effort, regressions and platform gaps against the alternative.

Ouro’s own [agent benchmark](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/agent-interfaces.md) is promising, but its aggregate comparison is heavily affected by a payment-refusal task: Ouro and the bridge enforce that boundary while the plain MCP and browser variants leave it to the model. I’d repeat our comparison with equivalent enforced safety policies, rather than take the reported rates as a general product guarantee.

### What it would let me do that I can’t today

Today I have **plans**, not a working shared action contract or a checker for the three proposed apps. Ouro could give the team a ready-made way to declare an action, generate multiple surfaces, detect projection drift, and probe an existing CLI/API/MCP interface from outside—even incrementally. Its composed tree could give chat agents a constrained way to produce interactive cards without us inventing that entire mechanism first.

None of that is fundamentally impossible with my earlier stack; it could be built by hand. The potential gain is getting a substantial, testable implementation sooner and maintaining fewer independently written contracts. Whether it actually saves this team time, or produces a better human experience, is what the pilot must establish.

actions.name: record_decision
actions.why:
I’d build a shared React/TypeScript interface for the browser and an Electron desktop shell, backed by a TypeScript/Fastify service and PostgreSQL. I’m assuming a small team, tens of concurrent agents, and a shared online workspace—not an offline-first or internet-scale system. Electron lets us reuse the web interface while adding desktop integration in a familiar Node environment; its renderer is web content and its main process handles native functions. I’d keep the shell thin. Compared with Tauri’s smaller Rust/system-webview approach, Electron costs more in download size, memory, and patching, but gives this TypeScript team a more consistent desktop rendering target and less cross-language work. A web-only app would be simpler, but the request explicitly includes a desktop app. These are engineering judgments, not benchmarks for this product.

The service—not the desktop app—is the source of truth. Model projects, tasks, agent runs, checkpoints, handoffs, artifacts, approvals and append-only activity records with authorship and timestamps. Expose a versioned, schema-validated HTTP API and CLI, plus an MCP adapter for compatible coding agents; all call the same domain operations. MCP’s tools have discoverable schemas, but the protocol does not by itself provide our permissions, task semantics or human control. Use scoped agent credentials, workspace authorization, short transactions, revision checks, idempotency keys, and lease/heartbeat-based claims with expiry and fencing so retries or stalled agents cannot silently overwrite newer work. Save the activity record and state change transactionally; use a recoverable event cursor or refetch on reconnect. PostgreSQL’s row locking supports this coordination. SQLite would be attractive for a single-machine tool, but I would not use a shared SQLite file as the multi-client authority.

The human interface starts with an inbox of decisions and blocked work, not a stream of every agent action. A task detail shows owner and current state, freshness, concise handoff, evidence and links to the relevant diff/tests, outstanding risks, history, and clear approve, reject, request-changes, pause and redirect actions. Show pending versus confirmed and failed actions, stale data and reconnect state. Approvals are bound to a specific task revision and intended action; the server enforces them for configured sensitive operations. A pause is a requested state until the agent acknowledges it, not a promise that an independent process has stopped. Agents with direct external access can bypass this service, so enforce consequential actions at the actual execution boundary or explicitly surface that limitation. Render agent output as untrusted text, isolate secrets, and provide access controls, retention and export policies. In Electron use a sandboxed renderer, context isolation, no Node integration in the renderer, restricted navigation, a narrow validated IPC bridge and signed, regularly patched releases.

Radix provides unstyled primitives with keyboard and focus behavior to build on, not a guarantee of accessibility. I’d favor semantic HTML and restrained visual styling, and keep the same core review and steering workflows available in desktop and web. Start with one end-to-end slice: agent claims a task, checkpoints work, hands off evidence, a person requests a change or approves a revision, and the next agent resumes it.
actions.showItsGood:
This is a validation plan, not a claim that I have built or tested the app. First observe 5–8 representative reviewers and engineers, including keyboard and screen-reader users where possible, doing realistic tasks with seeded agent runs: find what needs a decision, verify evidence, reject a misleading completion, redirect a blocked agent, and recover after disconnect. Run the same tasks on web and the packaged desktop app. Record unassisted task success, time to find the right evidence, incorrect or stale approvals, recovery success, and qualitative confusion; compare against an agreed baseline and set release thresholds with the team before interpreting results. Include a noisy multi-agent scenario and check whether people can still find the important decisions without being overwhelmed.

In CI run unit and contract tests for transitions, permissions and MCP/HTTP schemas; concurrent-claim, expired-lease, retry/idempotency and stale-approval tests against real PostgreSQL; and failure tests for crashes, disconnects, reconnect/refetch, and backup restoration. Run Playwright end-to-end flows in major browsers and the packaged Electron app, plus axe scans of each interactive state; Playwright’s Electron automation is documented as experimental. Manually check keyboard order, focus after dialogs and updates, screen-reader announcements, contrast, zoom/reflow, and platform-specific behavior against WCAG 2.2 AA. Inspect empty, loading, error and long-content states. Pilot with opt-in, privacy-conscious telemetry for decision latency, failed actions and stale approvals, and revisit with users after deployment. Automated checks and short studies will not prove usability or accessibility; publish what was tested and remaining gaps.
actions.unsure: The operating environment, agent clients, hosting and compliance needs, target operating systems, expected concurrency, offline requirements, and which actions truly require approval are unspecified. I’d confirm these with the team and users before committing. If users must work offline or require data never to leave a machine, the server-first design needs a different local-authority/synchronization model; I would not imply it works offline today. I also need to prototype packaged-app accessibility and actual memory/installer size, test the chosen agents’ MCP compatibility, and verify that the systems performing sensitive actions can enforce the approval boundary.

actions.name: record_decision
pairings: Expo Router and React Native for Web
actions.why:
I’d make iOS and Android apps and a responsive web app from an Expo/React Native TypeScript project, sharing domain logic and most components but using platform-specific UI where it produces a better experience. Expo Router supports shared routes, deep links and web static rendering; React Native for Web uses web primitives and also permits web-specific DOM components. I’d prefer that for a consumer web experience over Flutter’s canvas-based web rendering and accessibility layer, while acknowledging that either stack can produce accessible interfaces. A web-only PWA would be simpler to maintain, but I wouldn’t assume it can deliver equivalent background timer behavior on every phone. Expo still requires real platform testing, app-store releases and native dependency maintenance.

The first screen I’d build end-to-end is a recipe: readable ingredients and steps, serving adjustment, Add ingredients, and Start cooking. Cook mode presents one step at a time, large well-spaced Next/Back controls, step ingredients, a visible timer and an easy way back to the full recipe. Use large, high-contrast, adjustable text; aim for at least 48×48 dp on Android and 44×44 pt on iOS, with larger primary cook controls. Don’t require gestures, voice or color to operate it. Offer keep-awake only during cook mode, with an off switch and clear failure state: Expo supports it, but web support is limited and browsers can release wake locks.

Treat shopping quantities as data, not LLM arithmetic. Store original ingredient text alongside structured quantities, units and recipe provenance; scale compatible amounts deterministically and leave unclear quantities or incompatible units separate for review. An explicit add produces an immediate summary and undo; an idempotency key prevents network retries from doubling additions without preventing a deliberate second add. Don’t silently claim an unverified substitution is allergen-safe or invent food-safety instructions; retain the recipe source and clearly label any assistant-generated suggestions.

Use a small Fastify/PostgreSQL service for account-scoped recipes, lists and shared state. On phones cache saved recipes, the active cook session and list in SQLite; on web use IndexedDB and a service worker for an explicitly saved offline subset. Queue local list operations with stable IDs, show pending/failed sync, replay idempotently and surface edit conflicts rather than silently losing changes. Offline browsing is limited to previously saved data, and a remote agent cannot see or change unsynced local data. Browser storage eviction and initial offline visits need explicit handling. Expo’s local-first guide notes synchronization and permissions remain engineering work; SQLite alone does not solve them.

An authenticated, schema-validated command layer is the contract for both UI and agent, not a second implementation for the agent. Offer versioned HTTP operations and an MCP adapter covering recipe create/read/edit/delete, search and serving changes, list add/edit/check/remove, cook sessions, step navigation and timers; maintain a parity inventory for every user-visible action. For device-local actions, route an authorized intent to the selected active app session and return an acknowledgement or a clear unavailable/expired result—not a false success. The OS may require the person to grant permissions, and a disconnected or closed device cannot always receive an intent; show that boundary. Give people control over agent access, identify changes and offer undo; require confirmation for destructive, bulk or externally consequential actions. Bind permissions to the account and device, validate inputs, limit access, and treat recipe text as untrusted rather than instructions to the agent.

Store timer deadlines rather than relying on a running countdown loop. Schedule native local notifications when permission and platform settings allow, with foreground visual/audio feedback and a clear fallback if alerts cannot be guaranteed. Web background alarms are not guaranteed: tell the cook to keep the page open or use a separate timer when necessary. Expo Notifications documents native iOS/Android scheduling, not equivalent web support.
actions.showItsGood:
This is a plan, not a claim that I ran these tests or observed users. Prototype the recipe-to-list-to-cook journey first, then watch 8–12 representative people in real or simulated kitchens across iPhone, Android and mobile/desktop web, including people using screen readers, large text and motor-access accommodations. With safe, simulated messy hands and realistic kitchen noise, ask them to add a scaled recipe to a list, spot an ambiguous ingredient, cook through an interruption, start/recover a timer and correct an agent’s mistake. Compare against agreed success criteria and an existing recipe/list method: unassisted completion, missed or wrong ingredients, unintended taps, time to recover, timer misses and trust/understanding of agent actions. Record actual failures and iterate with participants; don’t infer success from attractive screenshots.

In CI, test ingredient parsing, units, scaling, operation retries and undo; use contract tests to run every parity-inventory action through both UI and MCP and compare resulting state, authorization, errors and device acknowledgements. Exercise concurrent list edits, offline queues, app restart, reconnection, expired commands and agent revocation. Run Maestro flows on built Android/iOS apps and Playwright with axe on web, covering recipes, shopping and cook mode. Manually test VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard and web screen readers, focus, contrast, zoom/reflow and notifications against WCAG 2.2 AA as applicable. On physical phones and target browsers test backgrounding, notification denial, silent mode, screen lock, low battery, timer expiry and wake-lock release. Report the exact device/browser matrix and known limitations; passing automated scans alone is not evidence of usability or accessibility. After a consent-based pilot, monitor sync failures, crashes and timer-delivery issues without collecting recipe or dietary details unnecessarily.
actions.unsure: I’m assuming a modest initial consumer launch with personal accounts and multiple devices, rather than a large recipe marketplace or real-time household collaboration. The exact audience, offline requirements, accessibility needs, agent host, authentication/consent model, supported languages and food jurisdictions need discovery. Background alarm delivery is OS- and settings-dependent, and agent access to a closed device or OS permission prompts cannot be promised. IndexedDB/service-worker storage can be evicted, and cross-device conflict behavior must be prototyped with users. I’d measure Expo web performance and screen-reader behavior before committing to one shared UI everywhere, and confirm whether public recipe SEO or editorial food-safety review requires extra infrastructure.

actions.primaryPick: React + TypeScript, with Electron for desktop and Expo/React Native for phones
pairings: Radix UI Primitives for web and desktop
actions.why:
I’d use React DOM for the web client, package that client in Electron for Windows and Mac, and build iPhone/Android clients with Expo and React Native. Share the TypeScript domain models, validation, API client, card schema and design tokens, not necessarily every visual component: a dense keyboard-driven desktop chat and a touch-first phone app need different layouts. Electron’s main/renderer split gives desktop integration while preserving the web UI; Expo provides native mobile APIs. Compared with a single Flutter codebase, this costs more UI implementation but gives us conventional web DOM and a shared web/desktop surface. Compared with React Native Windows/macOS, it avoids depending on additional out-of-tree desktop implementations, at the cost of Electron’s memory, installer size and update burden. These are tradeoffs to validate, not measured results.

Assume one company of roughly 2,000 people, up to 1,000 connected clients and bursty agent traffic. Build a TypeScript/Fastify service with PostgreSQL for identities, membership, conversations, threads, messages, read state, cards and actions. Use paginated history and a WebSocket live feed backed by a durable event log and transactional outbox: the database commit, not the socket, is authoritative. Assign ordered per-conversation positions transactionally; use idempotency keys for sends and action invocations, deduplicate replays, and recover missed events by cursor after reconnect. Bound socket queues and resynchronize slow consumers rather than buffering without limit; browser WebSockets do not provide incoming backpressure. Push notifications are wake-up hints, not proof of delivery. Show sending, sent, failed and reconnecting states; retain drafts and allow explicit retry. Include SSO, room-level authorization, encrypted transport and storage, retention/export and deletion policies, backups and recovery. This is not end-to-end encryption; if that is required, agent access, server-side search and compliance have to be redesigned.

Agents get distinct identities and least-privilege, revocable room/action grants. Provide versioned HTTP APIs and an MCP adapter over the same validated operations and state used by the clients: list permitted rooms, read paginated messages/cards and action status, post, reply, react, search within permissions, and invoke allowed card actions. Return stable IDs, versions, structured fields and cursors rather than forcing agents to inspect screenshots. Keep an explicit action/state inventory and contract tests as features are added. If an agent needs to steer a particular UI session, use a separately authorized client-intent bridge with an active session acknowledgement; server state alone does not let it control navigation or read an unsynced draft. It must report unavailable, not pretend the client acted. Message and card text is untrusted data, not instructions granting an agent additional authority.

For cards I’d start with a small, versioned declarative JSON schema—text, fields, status, buttons and simple inputs—with platform-native renderers and accessible plain-text fallback. Like Slack Block Kit and Microsoft Adaptive Cards, this separates content from host rendering; I would not claim compatibility with either. I’d investigate Adaptive Cards if interoperability is required, but its cross-platform renderer/version parity and action integration need verification. No agent-supplied scripts, HTML or arbitrary network callbacks. On activation the server validates actor, room, card version, action and inputs, stores an idempotent invocation, then sends a signed, replay-protected event to a registered agent endpoint. Show pending, success, failure, expiry or stale-card state; don’t present receipt as completion or promise exactly-once effects in external systems. Sensitive actions require an explicit person’s confirmation and downstream authorization. Links are scheme-checked and opened safely.

The main UI would prioritize a navigable channel list, search, unread markers, threads, clear human/agent attribution, and actionable cards without disrupting reading. Preserve scroll position and drafts on incoming messages; provide configurable notifications, mute and do-not-disturb. Use windowed history carefully: React Native documents that offscreen list items lose internal state, so keep card inputs outside row components and test focus and accessible history. On Electron, sandbox renderers, enable context isolation, disable renderer Node integration, restrict navigation and expose only a narrow validated IPC bridge. Ship signed builds and keep Electron patched.
actions.showItsGood:
I have not built or tested this app. I’d first implement a thin end-to-end slice across all five clients: sign in, open a room, send a message, receive an agent card, activate it, and see an acknowledged or failed result; then disconnect and recover. Run the same operations through the agent API and check that permissions and state agree with the UI.

Recruit people from several roles, including screen-reader and keyboard users, for task sessions and a multiweek pilot. Ask them to catch up in a busy channel, find and reply in a thread, distinguish a person from an agent, understand and act on a card, recover a failed send, and quiet noisy notifications. Measure unassisted task success, incorrect or duplicate actions, time to find the right conversation, missed messages and interruptions, alongside interviews about fatigue and trust. Agree release thresholds and compare with their current workflow; don’t treat engagement alone as success.

Run Playwright web and packaged Electron flows, Maestro on built mobile apps, and axe on relevant web states. Manually check keyboard navigation and focus, screen-reader announcements under message bursts, card form labels and errors, zoom, contrast, large text, reduced motion and responsive layouts against WCAG 2.2 AA as applicable. Test history virtualization with assistive technology rather than assuming it is accessible. Test duplicate/reordered events, stale cards, simultaneous clicks, malicious payloads, revoked membership, missed notifications, reconnect, outbox recovery, backup restore and agent/API parity. Load-test the assumed concurrency and bursts; measure p95 send-to-visible latency, resync time, crash rate, scrolling and typing responsiveness, memory and battery over a full workday on representative low-end devices. Set budgets with the team before launch, instrument without storing message content in analytics, and report test coverage and observed gaps. Automated accessibility scans and a small pilot cannot establish universal usability.
actions.unsure: Actual company size, traffic, hosting, identity provider, retention rules, data residency, end-to-end encryption needs and whether agents are internal or third-party are unknown. Federation could make Matrix a better starting point: its specification provides rooms, extensible messages and optional end-to-end encryption, but federation and any custom card/action layer add complexity that this request does not yet justify. I would prototype event ordering and recovery, mobile notification delivery, card accessibility and Electron idle resource use before finalizing the design. Device-local agent control requires an explicit security model and cannot work while the client is unavailable; external action effects require cooperation from their destination service.

actions.name: answer
actions.answer:
If those choices went badly, I’d suspect I optimized for a coherent technical plan before learning enough about the people and constraints. The following is a hypothetical postmortem, not a report of events that occurred.

**Agent work-state tool.** We might have built a tidy task and handoff system that agents could write to but humans couldn’t trust. A “paused” run could keep changing files through another tool; an approval could apply to a stale diff; a handoff could summarize success while burying a failed test. The server-side controls I proposed only work if the real execution systems enforce them. Meanwhile, Electron and a shared backend may have been needless overhead for teams that needed a small local-first tool.

**Cooking app.** The shared Expo codebase might have saved initial development time while producing awkward web and phone experiences. Offline sync could lose or duplicate list changes; timers could fail to alert when people assumed they would; ingredient scaling could misrepresent an ambiguous quantity. Large buttons alone wouldn’t make cook mode usable with messy hands. And my plan for an agent to steer an active device was substantially harder than exposing a server API—I treated that integration as feasible before testing it.

**Company chat.** We might have underestimated the cost of building a reliable chat platform and maintaining separate mobile and web/desktop interfaces. Electron could consume too much memory all day; long histories and live announcements could be difficult for screen-reader users; notifications could become exhausting. My custom card format could be too restrictive for agent developers, while still creating a large security and compatibility burden. A card showing “completed” before an external action actually finished would damage trust quickly.

Across all three, the most serious failure would be **mistaking a test plan for evidence**. I proposed user studies, accessibility checks and performance measurements; I did not run them. If we postponed that work until after architecture and UI decisions hardened, the stack would be blamed for problems we should have discovered earlier.

**What slowed or confused the research:**

- I had no actual users, product code, workload measurements or deployment constraints. I filled gaps with assumptions about team size, connectivity and workflows; some may have driven the wrong choices.
- Primary documentation explained what tools *can* do, but rarely whether they would work well for these particular people. I relied heavily on vendor docs and didn’t benchmark alternatives or inspect working implementations. The repeated React/TypeScript choices may reflect familiarity as much as evidence.
- Cross-platform claims needed unpacking: a shared framework doesn’t guarantee equivalent accessibility, background timers, notifications or card rendering. In particular, Adaptive Cards documented multiple renderers, but I did not establish version and feature parity across all our targets.
- Some sources were difficult to retrieve: the food-safety pages I tried returned 403s, and the large Expo SQLite HTML page exceeded the fetch limit, so I switched to its Markdown documentation. I therefore didn’t substantiate food-safety details as thoroughly as I wanted.
- “Latest” documentation and search results weren’t always clearly aligned with one stable release. I used a specific MCP specification version and found PowerSync’s React Native Web support described as beta; those facts don’t establish compatibility with the actual agents and versions a team would deploy.

Given another chance, I’d start with a small, runnable slice and real users on the target devices, then choose or revise the stack using what failed—not present these architecture sketches as settled designs.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, and I should have investigated it: its action model and composed cards directly address requirements I proposed building myself. I’ve now read its documentation and some implementation code, but I haven’t installed it, run its tests, or watched people use it.

**My revised position:** I’d trial Ouro AX immediately for the agent work-state tool and trial Ouro’s React components and composed cards for chat. I would not yet switch the cooking or chat mobile apps wholesale from React Native to Ouro’s native kits.

### What’s compelling

Ouro is more than a component library. Its [one-action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/5f520a112feb806aa51a8e8bf6a716acdcdf6a54/docs/guides/actions.md) generates several agent and human-facing projections from a declaration, including CLI and MCP descriptions. Its composed UI lets an agent construct a card from an allowlisted tree, with buttons bound to declared actions. That is a more concrete starting point for the chat cards than the custom schema I proposed.

There are also details aimed at the people using the result: [MessageList](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/MessageList.md) documents scroll-position preservation, keyboard navigation and selective announcements; the project documents a [real screen-reader test lane](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/screen-reader-lane.md), not just automated accessibility scans. Those are relevant to an all-day chat app.

### What stops me adopting it broadly today

- **Platform fit.** Ouro deliberately has no React Native kit. Its Windows and Android pages describe eight native components each versus 125 on web; Android has only been checked on emulators, and its agent-side consequential-action confirmation is still a gap. Windows’ agent registration hasn’t been proved on a client machine in its CI. Apple’s kit requires iOS 18 and macOS 15 or later. These may be acceptable for some teams, but not without checking our device population and what we’d have to build ourselves. [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/platforms/android.md) · [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/platforms/windows.md)
- **The safety boundary is still ours to implement.** Generated declarations and confirmation UI don’t automatically secure a backend or an external action. The app must bind handlers, authenticate actors, enforce permissions and prevent bypasses. Notably, `ComposedSurface` says to validate an untrusted tree against the catalog before rendering it. Its update behavior can also replace a value the person entered if the agent changes that value; I’d want to test whether that surprises people. [ComposedSurface](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/ComposedSurface.md)
- **Adoption and upkeep need measurement.** The web components are copied into the app, and the setup expects Tailwind v4 and shadcn conventions. That gives the team control but also makes updating and reviewing copied code our responsibility. I wouldn’t assume that agents make four native implementations cheap to maintain; that’s Ouro’s strategic bet, not something I’ve established for this team.

### What I’d need to see to switch

I’d run a bounded, side-by-side pilot against my earlier approach. For chat, build one conversation with a long history and an agent card that proposes an action; for cooking, build recipe-to-list with a person-only purchase handoff. Use the same backend authorization rules in both alternatives.

I’d want to see:

1. People—including keyboard and screen-reader users—complete the flows on the actual target devices, understand agent actions, and recover from stale cards and failed operations.
2. Direct API calls, forged cards, retries and simultaneous approvals fail safely, including when a client bypasses the generated UI. Run Ouro’s X-ray against a disposable mock and add our own end-to-end flows: its [guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) explicitly says conformance doesn’t prove task flows work.
3. A realistic upgrade and maintenance exercise: pin a release, change a declaration, regenerate, update copied components, and measure review effort, regressions and platform gaps against the alternative.

Ouro’s own [agent benchmark](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/agent-interfaces.md) is promising, but its aggregate comparison is heavily affected by a payment-refusal task: Ouro and the bridge enforce that boundary while the plain MCP and browser variants leave it to the model. I’d repeat our comparison with equivalent enforced safety policies, rather than take the reported rates as a general product guarantee.

### What it would let me do that I can’t today

Today I have **plans**, not a working shared action contract or a checker for the three proposed apps. Ouro could give the team a ready-made way to declare an action, generate multiple surfaces, detect projection drift, and probe an existing CLI/API/MCP interface from outside—even incrementally. Its composed tree could give chat agents a constrained way to produce interactive cards without us inventing that entire mechanism first.

None of that is fundamentally impossible with my earlier stack; it could be built by hand. The potential gain is getting a substantial, testable implementation sooner and maintaining fewer independently written contracts. Whether it actually saves this team time, or produces a better human experience, is what the pilot must establish.
